whisper_segs.text: Good morning, it's 7 o'clock on Friday the 6th of March.
This is Morning Ireland with Gavin Jennings and Sarah McInerney.
Today, more bombing of Tehran and Beirut.
The latest on trains in Dublin, women's sheds, the arrest of Brittany, the Welsh in town, and Meath Woman wins big at the RTE Choice Music Awards.
In business, oil prices up almost 18% in a week, and salary expectations are women asking less than men.
In sport, the Irish men's and women's hockey teams are each just one game away from World Cup qualification, and we preview Ireland versus Wales tonight in the Six Nations.
We're here with you until nine here on RT Radio 1 and the RT News Channel.
The news is read now by Susan Jackson.
The U.S.
President Donald Trump has said that it would be what he called a waste of time to currently consider sending U.S.
Ground troops into Iran.
He was dismissing the Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Arachi's prior warning that such a move would spell disaster for the U.S.
It comes as Israel said it launched a wave of strikes on the Iranian capital Tehran early this morning.
Iran also launched fresh strikes on Tel Aviv overnight.
Earlier, the U.S.
And Israel said they were moving into a new phase of their war on Iran.
U.S.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hexett said the attacks would intensify and said that their firepower over Iran was about to expand dramatically.
We have only just begun to fight and fight decisively.
If you think you've seen something, just wait.

The amount of combat power that's still flowing, that's still coming, that we'll be able to project over Iran is a multiples of what it currently is right now when you add up our capabilities and those of the Israeli Defense Forces.
In just days of Operation Epic Fury, you and your team have delivered nothing short of devastating, precise strikes, taking out...
The better part of Iran's navy, making it combat ineffective, neutralizing missile sites and launchers, and establishing...
dominance over the skies we fly over and seas we fly over.
Our forces are executing with unmatched skill, and the mission is advancing decisively.
The United States has eased its embargo on Russian oil after prices rose because of the Iran war.
The U.S.
Treasury Secretary said he was granting India a 30-day waiver to buy sanctioned Russian oil in an effort to sustain flows in the global market.
More measures to ease fuel costs are expected to be announced later today by the White House.
At home, St Patrick's National School in Selbridge will reopen on Monday after its Board of Management received written confirmation from the Department of Education that the building is safe.
Parents were given the news by the chair at a meeting last night.
The school announced earlier this week that it was closing temporarily due to structural defects and health and safety concerns.
Some travel news and in Dublin, DART services have resumed this morning following major disruption yesterday.
However, there's reduced capacity on a number of services.
Andrew Louth reports.

The 78-year-old founder of the now-defunct Apple Daily newspaper was found guilty in February on charges of foreign collusion and seditious publication.
His sentence is the harshest penalty so far under a national security law imposed by Beijing on Hong Kong following widespread pro-democracy protests.

Gardaí and emergency services attended the scene on the N33 at Capox Green near Arde yesterday afternoon.
The man who was the driver of the car was taken to Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital in Drogheda, where he was later pronounced dead.

keep up with online trends harming children and are seeing horrific cases where pupils are unable to escape bullies on social media.

and that only 57% of 3,000 adults surveyed have paid TV subscriptions from traditional providers such as Sky and Virgin.

21 are off to the Riviera, the headline reports today.
That's at least 21 state employees, including council officials.
A war-related story gives the Irish Daily Mirror and Irish Daily Star their leads.
The second flight bringing Irish citizens home from the Middle East, which arrived last night, and the joyous scenes as they were welcomed at Dublin Airport.
Its great Dubai home is the star headline.
The Irish Times looks ahead in its lead story.

President Donald Trump has demanded a say in picking Iran's next leader, despite scant signs that the regime is losing its grip in the face of a relentless U.S.
And Israeli air campaign.
Maniacal Trump's Iran pressure cooker explodes, says the headline over a column in the Times by Dermot Ferreter.
The historian describes the U.S.
Leader's actions on Iran as reality TV foreign policy, which does not actually merit the description policy.

Patrick's Day.
So far, she writes, Labour has been the only party to suggest that he should not take up the opportunity of the White House visit.
But the voices imploring him to do much more than sit there deferentially are growing louder.
Regan quotes what the Taoiseach said on this subject in a recent interview.
Diplomacy is not an endorsement of people.
Politically engaging with people is not an endorsement of the stance they have, he said.
But she says that the meeting the German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had in the Oval Office this week shows there are dangers in this approach too.
His failure to challenge Trump
has damaged him domestically and reportedly left a sour taste among other EU countries.
Yes, indeed, John.
Thank you very much for that.
Dangerous in every approach for Michael Martin when it comes to St.
Patrick's Day.
We've lots to come this hour.
We're going to get the latest on Irish Rail Service.
After some disruption, Britney Spears arrested under suspicion of driving under the influence of alcohol and drugs.
And up next, as the US says the fight has only just started, what next for the war in Iran?
A second attempt in as many days to rein in the war powers of US President Donald Trump has been rejected by US lawmakers.
Meanwhile, far from seeking to wind down military activity, the US Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, said yesterday that America had only just begun to fight.

Just before we came on air, I spoke with our Washington correspondent, Jackie Fox, and I began by asking her what happened in that second failed attempt by Congress to put a halt to Donald Trump's war powers.

Yes, so now both the Senate and the House of Representatives voted against measures that could have limited Donald Trump's ability to order further military action in Iran, effectively giving President Trump the green light to proceed with his campaign.
So Democrats have argued that Donald Trump did not have the authority to launch this operation because Congress is the only branch of government that can officially declare war.
This possibly isn't the end of this, though.
If this conflict continues, more measures could be put on the table because it's going to end up costing more money.
War is expensive.
We have a figure from the Centre of Strategic and International Studies that said the first 100 hours.
of Operation Epic Fury, estimated to cost $3.7 billion.
It's also going to cost more lives.
And this will turn into a pocketbook issue with the cost of energy going up due to this operation.
And all of that could change representatives'minds.
Because remember, we are in an election year.
The midterms are in November and all members of the House are up for re-election.
The economy and inflation are still major concerns.
Yeah, and of course, Donald Trump got elected on a peace platform.
So what do we know about American public opinion of what he's done here and the war?
That's right.
He said he is the America first president.
So the latest polling that we have is from CNN and it was conducted just after the strikes.
And it said about 60 percent of Americans disapproved of the attacks.
It'll be interesting to see what polling comes out over the weekend as American lives have been lost since that polling and those energy prices that we were talking about going up.
I think the Trump administration is aware that gas prices could be a problem here.
It said yesterday that India can now temporarily buy oil from Russia.
And Donald Trump suggested that the U.S.
Navy could escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz, which is that vital oil shipping lane.
Now, I spoke to some people in D.C.
Yesterday to see what they make of it all.
I think I've grown up my entire life watching us attack other people in other countries and not take it.
care of vets and ourselves, and I'm just sick of it.
Do you think President Trump overstepped his authority when it came to launching this operation in the first place?
Yeah, I mean, I think he's always done that.
If there's one person who oversteps, it's that man.
And frankly, I don't really have any faith in our Congress to do anything about it.
I think it's a good thing.
It's about time somebody cracked down on them.
And I think Trump's doing a good job as far as that.
See, because he has no fear.
All other presidents was like backing off.
But Trump gets it done.
There you go.
That is interesting.
Meanwhile, then we have British Prime Minister Keir Starmer joining calls for the U.S.
To reach a deal with Iran.
Jackie, but the U.S.
Administration seems to be taking an opposite approach.
They're saying things are only getting started.
A lot of talk this week, Sarah, about ramping up the operation.
Donald Trump saying that the U.S.
Is striking Iranian drone and missile systems every single hour.
By Thursday, we heard that the U.S.
Struck 2,000 targets and sunk 20 Iranian ships.
U.S.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had a lot to say about the operation during the week.

You can hear some of him now.
We have only just begun to fight and fight decisively.
If you think you've seen something, just wait.

The amount of combat power that's still flowing, that's still coming, that we'll be able to project over Iran is multiples of what it currently is right now when you add up our capabilities and those of the Israeli Defense Forces.
And just to pick up on that, Sarah, the U.S.
Is burning through its stock of precision weapons.
And what that means is it may need to prioritize what target it intercepts over the coming days.
The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Dan Kane, said that the U.S.
Rely on its larger stores of less sophisticated weapons as Iranian defenses are degraded in the coming days.
And White House officials also say that Donald Trump is meeting U.S.
Defense executives later today to discuss weapons production, including accelerating it.
And meanwhile, then we have attacks continuing on other Gulf states from Iran.
And yesterday, then we saw a missile being shot down before it reached Turkey.
Are there any concerns at all in the US about this conflict escalating and expanding?
Yes, we've seen the threat of this war spreading already, targets being hit throughout the Middle East, the Indian Ocean with the sinking of the Iranian ship by the US.
And as you said, Turkey said NATO air defences shot down an Iranian ballistic missile over the eastern Mediterranean as it was headed towards Turkey.
Iran's military denied launching that missile.
It said it respected the sovereignty of its neighbours.
But it is something that...
has rattled the region as an attack against Turkey, a NATO member, would dramatically escalate the conflict.
And it could raise the prospect of triggering NATO's Article 5 clause.
That is, you know, an attack on one member state can be considered an attack on all.
Now, I was on Capitol Hill yesterday.
Ahead of that House of Representatives vote on reining in the president's ability to launch further attacks on Iran.

I spoke to Republican Congressman Russell Fry from South Carolina and asked him his reaction to Europe's top diplomat, Kaya Callas'comments that this operation is leading to a dangerous moment for Europe.
The Iranian government for a long time has been very hostile, not only to Israel, but the United States, but really the entire West.
And you're seeing that play out in real time right now.
We saw NATO air defences shoot down what was described as an Iranian ballistic missile yesterday that was headed towards Turkish airspace.
Are you concerned that Article 5 of NATO could be triggered here as a result of this operation?
Look, I think broadly NATO and the West and all of our allies and partners, they face a heightened threat environment right now, given what is going on in Tehran.
So we need to be vigilant.
I'm not sure.
If Article 5 is, but obviously if there's a problem, NATO comes to each other's defense.
And Turkey is a NATO member.
Correct.
So the biggest fear that I have is what happens if Iran were to ever have a nuclear capability.
And that, I think, is where the president is at, is removing that potential.
In the midst of all this chaos then, Jackie, we have Christine Ohm being removed from her position as Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.
And of course, this comes after her appearance in front of the House Judiciary Committee.
Can you tell me, Jackie, what has happened here, do we know?
Yes, so Chrissie Noem, she's one of the most high profile cabinet members who really embraced the crackdown on immigration.
And she's been fired as the head of the Department of Homeland Security.
And this job oversees everything from cyber security to natural disasters to the Secret Service.
Many people were surprised she was allowed to stay on this long.
And the firing was just a day after some of those really tough questions and grillings at congressional hearings.
Now, it's thought Donald Trump was unimpressed by those hearings, particularly her statements that Mr.
Trump had approved tens of millions of dollars of government ads in which she was prominently featured.
And President Trump later denied that.
The uproar over those ads came as there was a lot of criticism, too, about her use of private jets.
And listen, she was on rocky ground for a while.
There was a lot of backlash when she called Alex Petty, who was shot and killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota.
He was a protester there protesting what ICE were doing in Minnesota.
And she called Alex Petty a domestic terrorist and refused to apologize yesterday about that on Capitol Hill.
She has been moved to a new role inside the administration.
It's called Special Envoy for the Shield of Americas, which would be a new security initiative for the Western Hemisphere.
Now, Democrats are refusing to approve more funds for the department that she once led, the Department of Homeland Security.
And it is in a third week of a shutdown.
Republicans have criticised this, citing more worries over terrorist threats due to the Iran conflict.
And I suppose they hope now that Chrystia Noem being removed will possibly get things back up and running at that department.
That was Jackie Fox speaking to me a little earlier on.
Later in the programme, we'll be hearing the views of people in Iran to this war and we'll be getting some more analysis on what happens now.

Women's sheds across the country are hoping a national umbrella organisation will put them on an equal footing when it comes to funding and support.
Unlike men's sheds,
Women's Sheds do not currently operate under a single national representative body, making it more difficult for them to avail of supports.

To mark International Women's Day on Sunday, Women's Sheds from across the country will gather for a conference in Tullamore this weekend to highlight the support network that Women's Sheds are now providing.

Becoming a national organisation is music to the ears of the Tullamore Women's Shed.

The women's shed movement has accelerated in recent years.

For many women, like Catherine Lockman, it provides a strong support network.
I think it's the most wonderful thing that's happened to me in years because I haven't been well.
And three years ago, I was diagnosed with an illness.
And the support I've got, the fact that people seem to care how you are or notice how you are, or if you seem to be quiet in yourself, you'll get a text or a visit or an invitation.
It's incredible.
I don't know how.
I don't know, it's a bit of an exaggeration to say I don't know how I'd have survived without it, but it's been wonderful for me.
We're generally not youngsters, so we've seen a bit of life and we know.
We can read the signs from others.
You know, there's more going on there maybe than they might want you to think of straight away.
You know, you can read a bit and that's where the support comes.
I mean, it's wonderful.

It's not the case, you know.
Despite their growing popularity, women's sheds have faced challenges.
Some have found it hard to find a permanent home.
And funding has always been an issue.
The Minister for Rural and Community Development, Derek O'Leary, has said he is committed to providing any support he can in the development of a national governing body.
That will put women's sheds on an equal footing with men's sheds and allow a representative body apply for more funding.
Jennifer Murnane O'Connor is Minister of State at the Department of Health with special responsibility for public health and wellbeing.

I have been working with Minister Derek O'Leary because in my own remit I have put aside funding now to put a structure together because we actually don't have a proper structure together for the women's sheds, but there is one for the men's sheds.

So it's a really important issue.
We have to make sure that we look after our women's sheds.
They do an excellent job.
